analysis.one_liner: Lets generic drug makers sue brand manufacturers that refuse to sell them samples needed for FDA testing.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it sat on the Senate calendar for nearly two years with 41 bipartisan cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes refuse to sell samples of their drugs to generic and biosimilar developers, who need those samples to run the tests FDA requires before approving a cheaper copy. The bill would let a blocked generic developer sue in federal court, get a judge's order requiring the brand maker to sell samples at cost-based prices, and recover attorney fees plus a penalty if the delay had no legitimate business reason. It would also let the FDA approve generic versions of tightly restricted drugs using a comparable safety program of the generic maker's own, instead of forcing the two companies to agree on one.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers, who pay high prices while brand drugs face no generic competition; and generic and biosimilar manufacturers, who would gain a legal path to the samples and safety-program agreements they need to bring lower-priced versions to market.

how_it_helps.text: A generic or biosimilar developer denied samples could sue and win a court order requiring the brand maker to sell the product at or below wholesale acquisition cost, with attorney fees and a monetary penalty if the delay lacked a legitimate business justification.

The bill cites FDA testimony that some manufacturers use safety programs and distribution restrictions as reasons not to sell samples, delaying generics, and FTC testimony about concern over these abuses.

It would let generic applicants use a 'different, comparable' safety program rather than being forced into a single shared program with the brand maker, removing a negotiation tactic that delays approvals.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, which currently profit from extended monopoly periods when generic testing is stalled, would face court orders, penalties up to the revenue earned during the delay, and faster generic competition.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a private right of action with financial penalties, which critics could expect to invite lawsuits and give courts a large role in drug-distribution disputes.
Allowing a generic maker to run its own comparable safety program instead of a single shared one raises patient-safety concerns the bill addresses by requiring FDA approval of the alternative system.
License holders are shielded from liability for misuse of the drug during the developer's testing, shifting safety risk during development onto the generic developer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is faster generic and biosimilar competition on drugs where samples are being withheld, which historically drives large price reductions; the costs are a new stream of litigation and some added FDA workload for approving alternative safety programs. The bill was narrowly tailored to the sample-blocking problem rather than a broad rewrite of drug law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar within a day, but the Senate never brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced February 5, 2019, with 28 original sponsors from both parties, and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar the next day.
It drew 41 cosponsors: 18 Republicans, 22 Democrats, and 1 Independent.
After being placed on the calendar under General Orders, no further action was taken and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without a Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: without a vote, they kept the ability to withhold samples and slow-walk shared safety-program negotiations, preserving months or years of extra monopoly pricing on affected drugs.

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of 28 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original introducer, giving the bill senior bipartisan sponsorship from both parties.

for.name: 41 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan support on paper.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the two years it sat on the calendar.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of brand drugs and biologics
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it undermined safety programs and created litigation risk, while lobbying against its passage.

sides.party_line_note: Support was split almost evenly across parties: 28 original sponsors included leading Democrats and Republicans, and the 41 cosponsors broke down as 18 Republicans, 22 Democrats, and 1 Independent; no roll-call opposition ever occurred because no vote was held.

industries.note: The bill targets the practice of withholding drug samples and stalling shared safety-program negotiations, tactics that extend monopoly pricing. Companies would lose that delay and face court orders and penalties tied to delay revenue.

Developers would gain a court-enforced right to buy samples at cost-based prices and an FDA pathway for their own comparable safety programs, letting them bring lower-priced competitors to market sooner.
